subject: MICRO
stem: A gram-positive coccus in clusters is catalase-positive and coagulase-positive. The most likely organism is:
explanation: S. aureus is catalase-positive and coagulase-positive. S. epidermidis is coagulase-negative, while streptococci and enterococci are catalase-negative. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 21.2 Bacterial Infections of the Skin and Eyes (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/21-2-bacterial-infections-of-the-skin-and-eyes).

subject: MICRO
stem: Which staining method is used to detect acid-fast bacilli such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
explanation: Ziehl-Neelsen (the hot acid-fast method; Kinyoun is the cold one) uses carbol fuchsin, acid-alcohol decolorizer, and methylene blue counterstain. AFB appear red. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 2.4 Staining Microscopic Specimens (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/2-4-staining-microscopic-specimens).

subject: MICRO
stem: The infective stage of Ascaris lumbricoides for humans is the:
explanation: Humans get infected by swallowing embryonated eggs. Filariform larvae are the infective stage of hookworms and Strongyloides, which penetrate skin. Reference: CDC DPDx, Ascariasis (cdc.gov/dpdx/ascariasis).

subject: MICRO
stem: Crescent- or banana-shaped gametocytes on a blood smear are characteristic of:
explanation: P. falciparum has crescent (banana-shaped) gametocytes. The other species have round gametocytes. Reference: CDC DPDx, Malaria (cdc.gov/dpdx/malaria).

subject: MICRO
stem: Which yeast is presumptively identified by a positive germ tube test?
explanation: Candida albicans (and C. dubliniensis) form germ tubes in serum after about 2–3 hours at 37 °C. Reference: Serum tube identification of Candida albicans (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC480459).

subject: MICRO
stem: The standard operating temperature of a steam autoclave is:
explanation: Autoclaves usually run at 121 °C (sometimes 132 °C) at 15–20 psi, typically for 20 minutes or more; the high temperature, not the pressure itself, kills endospores. 72 °C for 15 s is HTST pasteurization, and up to 170 °C for at least 2 hours is dry heat. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 13.2 Using Physical Methods to Control Microorganisms (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/13-2-using-physical-methods-to-control-microorganisms).

subject: MICRO
stem: Cultures of Mycobacterium tuberculosis are handled at which biosafety level?
explanation: BSL-3 covers pathogens such as M. tuberculosis, Bacillus anthracis, and West Nile virus; BSL-4 is for agents like Ebola, Marburg, and smallpox viruses. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 13.1 Controlling Microbial Growth (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/13-1-controlling-microbial-growth).

subject: MICRO
stem: HIV makes a DNA copy of its RNA genome using which enzyme?
explanation: HIV is a retrovirus: reverse transcriptase copies its RNA genome into DNA, which is then integrated into the host cell's DNA. This enzyme is the target of reverse transcriptase inhibitors such as AZT. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 14.4 Mechanisms of Other Antimicrobial Drugs (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/14-4-mechanisms-of-other-antimicrobial-drugs).

subject: MICRO
stem: A positive HBsAg result means that the person:
choices: Is infected with hepatitis B virus and is infectious
Recovered from a past infection and is immune
Has never been exposed to HBV
explanation: HBsAg indicates an infectious person. Anti-HBs alone means immunity from vaccination; anti-HBc means past or current infection (vaccines do not produce it). Reference: CDC, Interpretation of Hepatitis B Serologic Test Results (cdc.gov/hepatitis-b/media/serologicchartv8.pdf).

subject: MICRO
stem: What is the correct order of reagents in the Gram stain?
explanation: Crystal violet is the primary stain, Gram's iodine the mordant, ethanol or acetone-alcohol the decolorizer, and safranin the counterstain. Leaving the decolorizer on too long can give false results. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 2.4 Staining Microscopic Specimens (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/2-4-staining-microscopic-specimens).

subject: MICRO
stem: Gram-positive bacteria stay purple after decolorization because they have:
choices: An outer membrane rich in lipopolysaccharide
A thick peptidoglycan layer in the cell wall
Mycolic acids in the cell wall
explanation: A thick peptidoglycan layer holds the crystal violet–iodine complex, so gram-positive cells resist the decolorizer. Gram-negative cells lose it and take up the pink safranin. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 2.4 Staining Microscopic Specimens (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/2-4-staining-microscopic-specimens).

subject: MICRO
stem: On mannitol salt agar, Staphylococcus aureus is recognized by:
choices: Growth in 7.5% NaCl with a yellow color change from mannitol fermentation
explanation: Staphylococci tolerate the 7.5% NaCl in the medium, and S. aureus ferments mannitol, producing acid that turns the medium yellow. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 21.2 Bacterial Infections of the Skin and Eyes (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/21-2-bacterial-infections-of-the-skin-and-eyes).

subject: MICRO
stem: A beta-hemolytic, catalase-negative coccus from a sore throat is susceptible to 0.04 units of bacitracin. It is most likely:
explanation: Streptococcus pyogenes (group A strep), the cause of strep throat, is beta-hemolytic and susceptible to 0.04 units of bacitracin. Staphylococci are catalase-positive. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 22.2 Bacterial Infections of the Respiratory Tract (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/22-2-bacterial-infections-of-the-respiratory-tract).

subject: MICRO
stem: Alpha-hemolytic, lancet-shaped gram-positive diplococci that are sensitive to optochin are most likely:
explanation: S. pneumoniae is an alpha-hemolytic streptococcus with lancet-shaped diplococcal morphology; it is extremely sensitive to optochin and its colonies are destroyed by sodium deoxycholate (bile). Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 22.2 Bacterial Infections of the Respiratory Tract (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/22-2-bacterial-infections-of-the-respiratory-tract).

subject: MICRO
stem: On MacConkey agar, a strong lactose fermenter grows as:
choices: Yellow colonies with a yellow halo
explanation: MacConkey agar has bile salts and crystal violet that inhibit many gram-positive bacteria, and lactose fermenters make acid that turns their colonies hot pink; non-fermenters stay colorless. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 9.6 Media Used for Bacterial Growth (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/9-6-media-used-for-bacterial-growth).

subject: MICRO
stem: Haemophilus influenzae grows on chocolate agar because it requires:
explanation: H. influenzae only grows on media that supply factor X (hemin) and factor V (NAD), such as chocolate agar. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 22.2 Bacterial Infections of the Respiratory Tract (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/22-2-bacterial-infections-of-the-respiratory-tract).

subject: MICRO
stem: The urea breath test detects Helicobacter pylori because the organism produces:
explanation: H. pylori, a major cause of peptic ulcers, produces urease that breaks down labeled urea, releasing labeled CO₂ in the breath. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 24.3 Bacterial Infections of the Gastrointestinal Tract (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/24-3-bacterial-infections-of-the-gastrointestinal-tract).

subject: MICRO
stem: A patient has profuse "rice-water" stools. Which medium is used to isolate the likely organism, and how does it grow?
explanation: Rice-water stool is typical of cholera. TCBS agar is selective and differential for Vibrio species, and V. cholerae forms distinct yellow colonies. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 24.3 Bacterial Infections of the Gastrointestinal Tract (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/24-3-bacterial-infections-of-the-gastrointestinal-tract).

subject: MICRO
stem: Mycobacteria are acid-fast mainly because their cell walls contain:
explanation: The mycobacterial cell wall is rich in waxy mycolic acids, which block ordinary Gram stain reagents, so a special acid-fast stain is needed. The waxy wall also makes them grow slowly. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 22.2 Bacterial Infections of the Respiratory Tract (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/22-2-bacterial-infections-of-the-respiratory-tract).

subject: MICRO
stem: The medium commonly used to culture Mycobacterium tuberculosis is:
explanation: M. tuberculosis grows on Löwenstein-Jensen agar as distinct colonies. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 4.4 Gram-Positive Bacteria (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/4-4-gram-positive-bacteria).

subject: MICRO
stem: A sputum culture for Mycobacterium tuberculosis is kept for several weeks before it is reported negative because the organism:
choices: Must first be converted to a yeast form
explanation: Its waxy mycolic acid wall makes M. tuberculosis grow slowly; visible colonies can take about four weeks to appear. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 4.4 Gram-Positive Bacteria (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/4-4-gram-positive-bacteria) and 22.2 (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/22-2-bacterial-infections-of-the-respiratory-tract).

subject: MICRO
stem: The Mantoux tuberculin skin test is read:
choices: After 48–72 hours, by measuring the hardened (indurated) area
explanation: Tuberculin protein derivative is injected into the skin, and the test is read 48–72 hours later by measuring the size of the hardened, responding area. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 22.2 Bacterial Infections of the Respiratory Tract (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/22-2-bacterial-infections-of-the-respiratory-tract).

subject: MICRO
stem: Interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) for TB infection are:
explanation: IGRAs are TB blood tests that use a blood sample to find out if a person is infected with TB bacteria. Reference: CDC, Testing for Tuberculosis (cdc.gov/tb/testing).

subject: MICRO
stem: The BCG vaccine against tuberculosis is based on a strain of:
explanation: The TB vaccine is based on the bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) strain of M. bovis, which is commonly found in cattle. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 22.2 Bacterial Infections of the Respiratory Tract (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/22-2-bacterial-infections-of-the-respiratory-tract).

subject: MICRO
stem: Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR TB) is caused by TB bacteria resistant to at least:
explanation: MDR TB is caused by TB bacteria that are resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampin, the two most important first-line drugs. Reference: CDC, Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis Disease (cdc.gov/tb/hcp/treatment/drug-resistant-tuberculosis-disease.html).

subject: MICRO
stem: In primary tuberculosis, healed, calcified lesions in the lung are called:
explanation: Infected alveoli become walled off into small round lesions called tubercles, and most lesions eventually heal into calcified Ghon complexes. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 22.2 Bacterial Infections of the Respiratory Tract (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/22-2-bacterial-infections-of-the-respiratory-tract).

subject: MICRO
stem: Which acid-fast staining method does NOT use heat to drive carbolfuchsin into the cells?
explanation: The Ziehl-Neelsen method uses heat to infuse carbolfuchsin into acid-fast cells, whereas the Kinyoun method does not use heat. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 2.4 Staining Microscopic Specimens (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/2-4-staining-microscopic-specimens).

subject: MICRO
stem: A dimorphic fungus typically grows as:
choices: A yeast at 25 °C and a mold at 37 °C
A mold at 25 °C and a yeast at 37 °C
A yeast only in anaerobic conditions
explanation: Dimorphic fungi switch form with temperature, for example growing as a mold at 25 °C and as yeast cells at 37 °C (body temperature). Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 5.3 Fungi (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/5-3-fungi).

subject: MICRO
stem: The three genera of dermatophytes are:
explanation: All three dermatophyte genera, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton, and Microsporum, can cause cutaneous mycoses (tineas). Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 21.4 Mycoses of the Skin (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/21-4-mycoses-of-the-skin).

subject: MICRO
stem: Why is potassium hydroxide (KOH) added to skin, hair, or nail scrapings for fungal examination?
choices: To dissolve keratin so the hyphae can be seen
To make yeast form germ tubes
explanation: KOH dissolves the keratin in hair, nails, and skin cells, which lets fungal hyphae be seen under the microscope. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 21.4 Mycoses of the Skin (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/21-4-mycoses-of-the-skin).

subject: MICRO
stem: Sabouraud dextrose agar with chloramphenicol and cycloheximide is used to:
choices: Culture dermatophytes while inhibiting bacteria and saprophytic fungi
explanation: This selective agar supports dermatophyte growth while inhibiting bacteria and saprophytic fungi. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 21.4 Mycoses of the Skin (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/21-4-mycoses-of-the-skin).

subject: MICRO
stem: A patient developed pneumonia after cleaning a cave full of bat droppings. The most likely fungus is:
explanation: The main reservoir of Histoplasma capsulatum is soil, especially soil rich in bat or bird feces. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 22.4 Respiratory Mycoses (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/22-4-respiratory-mycoses).

subject: MICRO
stem: Aspergillosis is most often caused by:
explanation: Aspergillosis is most often caused by Aspergillus fumigatus or A. flavus; Aspergillus bears its conidia (spores) on conidiophores. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 21.4 Mycoses of the Skin (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/21-4-mycoses-of-the-skin) and 5.3 Fungi (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/5-3-fungi).

subject: MICRO
stem: Pneumocystis pneumonia is seen most often in:
choices: Patients with AIDS and other immunocompromised patients
People who keep birds as pets
explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii is a leading cause of pneumonia in patients with AIDS. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 22.4 Respiratory Mycoses (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/22-4-respiratory-mycoses).

subject: MICRO
stem: In tissue, which fungus forms spherules filled with endospores?
explanation: Once inside the body, Coccidioides differentiates into spherules that are filled with endospores. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 22.4 Respiratory Mycoses (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/22-4-respiratory-mycoses).

subject: MICRO
stem: An India ink preparation is used to show the capsule of:
explanation: India ink, a negative stain, shows the large capsules around Cryptococcus yeast cells in lung tissue or cerebrospinal fluid. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 22.4 Respiratory Mycoses (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/22-4-respiratory-mycoses).

subject: MICRO
stem: The best way to diagnose pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis) infection is:
choices: Transparent tape pressed on the perianal skin in the morning
A blood smear taken at midnight
explanation: Cellulose tape is applied to the anus in the morning before the first bowel movement to pick up the eggs, which are slightly flattened on one side. Reference: CDC DPDx, Enterobiasis (cdc.gov/dpdx/enterobiasis).

subject: MICRO
stem: Humans get hookworm infection mainly through:
choices: Filariform larvae in soil penetrating the skin
explanation: Filariform (third-stage) larvae in the environment infect humans by penetrating the skin. Reference: CDC DPDx, Hookworm (cdc.gov/dpdx/hookworm).

subject: MICRO
stem: Human cysticercosis is acquired by:
choices: The bite of an infected fly
explanation: Cysticercosis is acquired only by swallowing T. solium eggs (fecal-oral route). Eating cysticerci in undercooked pork causes intestinal taeniasis instead. Reference: CDC DPDx, Cysticercosis (cdc.gov/dpdx/cysticercosis).

subject: MICRO
stem: Schistosome eggs with a prominent terminal spine, found in urine, belong to:
explanation: S. haematobium eggs have a conspicuous terminal spine and are shed in urine. S. mansoni eggs have a lateral spine, and S. japonicum eggs have a small, inconspicuous spine. Reference: CDC DPDx, Schistosomiasis (cdc.gov/dpdx/schistosomiasis).

subject: MICRO
stem: Which Schistosoma species is found in the Philippines?
explanation: S. japonicum is found in China, the Philippines, and Sulawesi; its eggs have a smaller, less conspicuous spine than other species. Reference: CDC DPDx, Schistosomiasis (cdc.gov/dpdx/schistosomiasis).

subject: MICRO
stem: How many nuclei does a mature Entamoeba histolytica/dispar cyst have?
explanation: Mature E. histolytica/E. dispar cysts have 4 nuclei. Ingested red cells in trophozoites suggest E. histolytica, but E. dispar can occasionally contain them too, so it isn't a reliable way to tell them apart. Reference: CDC DPDx, Amebiasis (cdc.gov/dpdx/amebiasis).

subject: MICRO
stem: Pear-shaped trophozoites with two large nuclei in a stool specimen suggest:
explanation: Giardia duodenalis trophozoites are pear-shaped with 2 large nuclei; the resistant cysts are responsible for transmission. Reference: CDC DPDx, Giardiasis (cdc.gov/dpdx/giardiasis).

subject: MICRO
stem: Capillaria philippinensis infection is acquired by:
choices: Eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish
explanation: C. philippinensis is endemic in the Philippines; humans are infected by eating raw or undercooked fish, the intermediate host. Reference: CDC DPDx, Intestinal Capillariasis (cdc.gov/dpdx/intestinalcapillariasis).

subject: MICRO
stem: Which process kills all microbes, including endospores?
explanation: Sterilization kills vegetative cells, endospores, and viruses. Disinfection of objects doesn't sterilize because endospores tend to survive, and antiseptics are chemicals safe for living skin or tissue. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 13.1 Controlling Microbial Growth (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/13-1-controlling-microbial-growth).

subject: MICRO
stem: Work with nonpathogenic strains of E. coli on an open laboratory bench corresponds to which biosafety level?
explanation: BSL-1 agents generally do not cause infection in healthy adults (e.g., nonpathogenic E. coli), and workers may handle them at an open bench. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 13.1 Controlling Microbial Growth (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/13-1-controlling-microbial-growth).

subject: MICRO
stem: Which biological safety cabinet is gas-tight with attached rubber gloves and is used for highly infectious BSL-4 agents?
explanation: Class III BSCs are designed for highly infectious agents like those in BSL-4 laboratories; the alternative at BSL-4 is a full-body positive-pressure suit. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 13.2 Using Physical Methods to Control Microorganisms (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/13-2-using-physical-methods-to-control-microorganisms).

subject: MICRO
stem: HEPA filters used in biological safety cabinets have an effective pore size of about:
explanation: HEPA filters have effective pore sizes of 0.3 µm, small enough to trap bacteria and many other particles in the air. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 13.2 Using Physical Methods to Control Microorganisms (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/13-2-using-physical-methods-to-control-microorganisms).

subject: MICRO
stem: Dry-heat sterilization of glassware in a hot-air oven typically uses:
explanation: Dry heat needs long exposure (at least 2 hours) at temperatures up to 170 °C in a dry-heat oven. 121 °C is moist heat (autoclave), and 72 °C for 15 s is pasteurization. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 13.2 Using Physical Methods to Control Microorganisms (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/13-2-using-physical-methods-to-control-microorganisms).

subject: MICRO
stem: High-temperature short-time (HTST) pasteurization of milk uses:
choices: 121 °C for 15 minutes, producing a sterile product
72 °C for 15 seconds, reducing but not eliminating microbes
explanation: HTST pasteurization exposes milk to 72 °C for 15 seconds. Pasteurization uses heat but does not make the food sterile. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 13.2 Using Physical Methods to Control Microorganisms (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/13-2-using-physical-methods-to-control-microorganisms).

subject: MICRO
stem: Plastic items such as gloves and IV tubing are commonly sterilized with:
explanation: Ionizing radiation is used clinically to sterilize gloves, IV tubing, and other latex and plastic items. UV light is nonionizing and does not penetrate surfaces, plastics, or glass. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 13.2 Using Physical Methods to Control Microorganisms (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/13-2-using-physical-methods-to-control-microorganisms).

subject: MICRO
stem: Why is 70% alcohol a better disinfectant than 100% alcohol?
choices: 100% alcohol is too flammable to use
Pure alcohol coagulates surface proteins too fast, blocking penetration into the cell
explanation: Alcohols work better in water: at high concentrations they rapidly coagulate surface proteins, which prevents effective penetration of the cell. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 13.3 Using Chemicals to Control Microorganisms (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/13-3-using-chemicals-to-control-microorganisms).

subject: MICRO
stem: Viruses are described as obligate intracellular parasites because they:
choices: Can grow on any nutrient agar
Can only replicate inside a living host cell
explanation: Viruses are acellular and must infect a cellular host to survive and reproduce, which makes them obligate intracellular parasites. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 6.1 Viruses (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/6-1-viruses).

subject: MICRO
stem: In viral cell culture, a cytopathic effect (CPE) is:
choices: A color change of the culture medium from bacterial growth
A visible abnormality of infected host cells
The antibody response of the patient
A clump of red cells caused by the virus
explanation: Cytopathic effects are distinct, observable cell abnormalities due to viral infection; their type and severity depend on the virus. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 6.3 Isolation, Culture, and Identification of Viruses (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/6-3-isolation-culture-and-identification-of-viruses).

subject: MICRO
stem: Which of these can be used to grow viruses in the laboratory?
explanation: Viruses need a living host cell, so they are grown in whole organisms, cell cultures, or the embryo inside an embryonated bird's egg, not on bacterial media. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 6.3 Isolation, Culture, and Identification of Viruses (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/6-3-isolation-culture-and-identification-of-viruses).

subject: MICRO
stem: Hepatitis A virus is mainly transmitted by:
explanation: HAV is generally spread by the fecal-oral route, close personal contact, or contaminated water or food, while HBV is linked to infectious blood or body fluids. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 24.4 Viral Infections of the Gastrointestinal Tract (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/24-4-viral-infections-of-the-gastrointestinal-tract).

subject: MICRO
stem: The two main surface spike antigens of influenza virus are:
explanation: Influenza's main antigens are the spike proteins hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N); changes in them by antigenic drift and shift produce new strains. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 22.3 Viral Infections of the Respiratory Tract (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/22-3-viral-infections-of-the-respiratory-tract).

subject: MICRO
stem: A patient has had dengue-like fever for 3 days. Which test best confirms a current infection at this stage?
explanation: NS1 antigen in serum during the first 7 days of illness indicates a current or recent dengue infection, and RT-PCR detects the RNA in days 0–7. IgM testing identifies most infections after day 3. Reference: CDC, Dengue Diagnosis and Testing (cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/diagnosis-testing).

subject: MICRO
stem: A person is anti-HBs positive but HBsAg and anti-HBc negative. This means:
choices: Immunity from a past natural infection
explanation: Anti-HBs alone means vaccine immunity. Past natural infection would also show anti-HBc, which vaccines do not produce. Reference: CDC, Interpretation of Hepatitis B Serologic Test Results (cdc.gov/hepatitis-b/media/serologicchartv8.pdf).

subject: MICRO
stem: HBsAg positive, total anti-HBc positive, and IgM anti-HBc positive, with anti-HBs negative, indicates:
explanation: HBsAg with IgM anti-HBc means acute infection; the same pattern with IgM anti-HBc negative means chronic infection. Reference: CDC, Interpretation of Hepatitis B Serologic Test Results (cdc.gov/hepatitis-b/media/serologicchartv8.pdf).
